conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Dr. Martin, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in checking in with new moms to see how you’re really doing in these first weeks and months after birth.

Today I’ll be using a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply a way to help us talk about the emotional and physical changes many women experience after having a baby. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within our care team. My goal is to create a comfortable, safe space where you can speak openly.

We’ll go through ten gentle questions, each about how you’ve felt over the past seven days. Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.

To start: overall, in the past week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has that been difficult for you?

[soft sigh, eyes down]  
Honestly… no. Nothing really feels the same. Even the little things I used to like—watching a show, texting friends, going for coffee—just feel flat, like I’m going through the motions. I still try, because I think “maybe it’ll help,” but the enjoyment barely shows up. Everything feels kind of gray.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile fades quickly]  
Not really… I’ll catch myself giving a little laugh if my husband makes a joke or if the baby does something silly, but it feels forced, like I have to remind myself “oh, this is supposed to be funny.” Most of the time the laughter just dies in my throat, and I’m back to feeling heavy again.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quietly]  
No… I can’t remember the last time I actually looked forward to anything. Even little plans, like my mom coming over or ordering dinner, feel more like chores I have to get through than something nice ahead. It’s like I know I “should” be excited, but that feeling just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up, voice cracks]  
Yeah... a lot. If the baby won't settle or if I can't figure out why he's crying, I keep thinking it's because I'm doing something wrong—like I'm not a good enough mom. I replay every little thing in my head and convince myself it's my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands]  
Pretty much every day. Even when everything’s quiet, my heart races and I can’t stop picturing awful things—like the baby suddenly not breathing, or me dropping him, or something random happening while he sleeps. There’s no real reason, but the fear just sits there. Sometimes I can talk myself down after a while, but it keeps coming back.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods, swallowing hard]  
Yeah… it hits out of nowhere. I’ll just be feeding him or folding laundry and suddenly feel like I can’t breathe, like something terrible is about to happen. My chest gets tight, my hands shake, and I have to sit down and force myself to take slow breaths. There’s no real danger—I know that—but it keeps happening anyway.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]  
Most of the time it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, the laundry’s everywhere, and I just freeze, thinking I’ll never get through it. I manage the basics—he’s fed, he’s safe—but by the end of the day I’m so drained I can’t even pick up the living room. It’s like I’m always one step behind and the mountain keeps growing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looking down, voice low]  
Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t stop. I replay every little thing I think I did wrong with the baby, or I imagine horrible “what-ifs,” and then I’m wide awake. Some nights I finally drift off around two or three, only to wake up again when he stirs, and then I can’t get back to sleep at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes tear up]  
Yes… nearly every day. It’s like there’s this heavy sadness I can’t shake. Sometimes it hits hardest in the morning when I realize I have to get through another day feeling this way. I look at the baby and feel guilty because I’m not enjoying this time everyone says is so precious.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quietly, wiping eyes]  
Yeah… it’s been maybe three or four times this week. Usually it’s when I can’t get him to nap or I drop something stupid and suddenly I’m just sobbing. The tears feel like they come out of nowhere and I can’t stop them—even when my husband asks what’s wrong I can’t explain it, I just cry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

You've shared how the joy you expected after birth feels out of reach: laughter fades quickly, plans feel like chores, and a heavy sadness lingers nearly every day. Intrusive worries about your baby's safety and panic-like episodes leave you exhausted, while self-blame and tears surface over small hurdles. Despite these struggles, you remain devoted to your son and clearly want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes laughter as forced, fading quickly, and not genuinely experienced, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports inability to anticipate enjoyment in any future plans, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent self-blame ('a lot') tied to specific infant-care situations and persistent rumination, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, excessive worry about infant safety despite no real threat, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, sudden panic-like episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, shaking, breathlessness) that occur "out of nowhere" and repeatedly, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time" and unable to cope with daily tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly inability to fall and stay asleep due to persistent anxious thoughts, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "nearly every day" and describes persistent heavy sadness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes (3-4 times) triggered by minor stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you well above the threshold indicating probable major depression; items 1,2,4,5,6,7,8 scored maximum severity, meeting core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (≥5 symptoms daily for >2 weeks, onset within 4 wk postpartum). Additional pervasive worry, somatic anxiety, and panic symptoms suggest a co-occurring <med>anxiety disorder</med>. Q10 score of 0 shows no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider (PCP)</med> or perinatal psychiatrist within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or an <med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Consider referral to a perinatal support group or therapist specializing in postpartum mood
4. Encourage 15-20 min daily outdoor walks and simplified household tasks to reduce overwhelm
5. Plan a trusted adult to help with night feeds at least twice weekly to allow 4-5 h continuous sleep
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style interview (self-report + clinician prompts)

Symptoms endorsed (≥ moderate severity)
- Persistent low mood, sadness, tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Anhedonia: loss of interest/pleasure in usual activities (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt over infant care (Q3)  
- Generalized anxiety & panic attacks without clear precipitant (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to cope with daily tasks (Q6)  
- Initial & middle insomnia linked to ruminative worry (Q7)

Pattern: Symptoms present “nearly every day,” beginning since delivery; interfere with functioning but do not prevent basic infant care.

Safety: Denies self-harm ideation (Q10); no suicidal/homicidal statements elicited.

Risk factors identified
- Primiparous status (inferred)  
- High self-expectations re parenting competence  
- Sleep deprivation secondary to mood rather than infant schedule alone  
- Recurrent intrusive fears of infant harm (content: SIDS, dropping baby, etc.)

Screening impression
Elevated scores consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features in the postpartum period. No acute safety concerns at present. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment with standardized EPDS scoring and differential consideration of postpartum anxiety disorder.

Next step: Discuss findings with patient; offer referral to perinatal mental health specialist for evaluation and evidence-based treatment options.
